units: the writer has settled not far from a harbor area
he lists the vehicles he has at hand
the boat belongs to his neighbor
he has learned to free the line that holds the boat
his bicycle is old and needs weekly upkeep
he uses it to reach the market
an animal pulls the cart
the craftsman strengthened the pulling gear
the shared boat leaves a trail on the water
the load he must move guides his choice
text: Dear friend, I am writing to set out for you the means of travel I have had at hand since settling close to the harbor. There are four of them, and each has its hour. The first is a boat that belongs to my neighbor, and I have learned to slip its mooring line free without fumbling at the knot. The second is an old bicycle, heavy in the frame, which I service every week without fail and ride down to the covered market. The third is a cart drawn by a donkey, whose harness the wheelwright strengthened for me before the cold weather set in. The fourth is the river ferry, which leaves a broad and quiet wake behind it. I confess that my choice depends above all on the load I must carry and on the state of the tracks. Please accept my sincere regards, and believe in my wish to welcome you here before long.

units: training opens with a spell of watching from the landing stage
the newcomer first learns to work the helm
he then sails as second hand on real crossings
approach drills happen over still water at first
a head wind is added to raise the difficulty
the examination includes a crossing made in the dark
a breakdown is staged on purpose during the test
the final landing is carried out without power
the certified pilot works under a veteran for one season
shipping owners distrust pilots who lack experience
text: How does anyone begin training as a river ferry pilot? It starts at the landing stage, where the trainee spends his days watching the maneuvers and learns to hold the helm without forcing it. What comes after that? The candidate ships out as second hand and repeats his approaches on real crossings, over still water at first, then against a head wind. Which tests close the course? A crossing made in the dark, a breakdown staged on purpose and a landing brought off without power. Why does that last one matter? It forces the crew to read the current and to watch the wash thrown up by passing vessels. Is the certificate enough to take command? No, the holder must still shadow an old hand through a whole season. Shipping owners welcome such caution, for they rarely hand a deck over to a beginner.

units: the courier takes off his head gear before speaking
a slippery layer covered the road surface
his two-wheeler lost its grip on a bend
the driving wheel spun without biting the ground
he insists that he did not fall
he weaved between heavy trucks to keep out of the ditch
a parcel came off the rear rack
he turned back to pick the parcel up
his delivery round ran late
he took a picture of the wheel to convince his boss
text: The delivery rider set his helmet down on the table and started talking. He told me the road had been coated all over with a thin slick of mud and that his scooter had slid out on the lower bend. The back wheel, he said, would spin without biting as soon as he opened the throttle at all. I asked him whether he had gone down, because he was limping a little on his way in. He said no, but he had weaved between two heavy trucks to keep himself out of the ditch. A parcel had worked loose from the rear rack, so he doubled back to pick it up, and the whole round ended up running late. His boss, he told me, never believes a word about mud. That is why he took a picture of the dirty wheel before setting off again, just to have something solid in hand. Then he shrugged and put the helmet back on.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: switching tracks once called for heavy hand labor
workmen had to lift the rolling stock and shove it across
the growing number of lines made the problem sharper
a workshop hand thought up a device with swinging blades
one pull on a lever was enough to move those blades
from then on the train changed course while still rolling
the system had few parts and was easy to mend
this invention helped lines grow into a network
students of technical history see it as a turning point
text: Long ago a train on rails could change course only at the cost of painful labor. Workmen levered the wheels up with a bar, then shoved the frame across by hand, so every branching point ate up real effort. Operators wanted a way out, for lines were multiplying and crossings came thick and fast. A mechanic in a repair shed hit on the idea of two hinged steel blades, held against the fixed rails, which a lever swung aside in a single motion. From then on the train swung onto the other track while still rolling. The method spread fast, because it used few parts and could be mended where it stood. It changed the shape of the lines themselves: builders stopped laying single stretches and wove webs in which each branch met the next. Historians of technology call it a founding gesture.

units: the two ways of moving look alike but spend energy differently
the walker must lift his own weight at every stride
his energy drains away in a movement he keeps repeating
the cyclist lets the saddle carry his weight
he keeps up a turning motion that the wheel holds on to
for the same effort the bicycle covers a greater distance
walking calls for no machinery at all
it gets over obstacles that a wheel cannot clear
the machine offers speed but stays fragile
the kind of ground should guide the traveler in his choice
text: Walking and cycling look like near neighbors, and yet they spend their energy in wholly different ways. The walker lifts his own weight at every stride, sets it down and lifts it again. His effort drains away into a stubborn beat. The cyclist hands that weight over to a saddle and has only to keep a circle turning, which the wheel carries on for him. Out of this comes a striking gap. For the same effort the bicycle takes its rider far beyond what his legs alone would manage. Walking keeps a quieter advantage. It asks for no chain, no inner tube, no smooth roadway, and it climbs the stair, the bramble, the loose sand. One buys speed and pays with a fragile machine. The other buys freedom and pays in slowness. A wise traveler reads the ground before he settles the question.

units: the customer reports a sway that shows up at high speed
the diagnosis is worked through station by station
the coupling part had too much play in it
that play set off jolts on a crowned road surface
the tires showed slanted wear along the inner edge
such wear points to wheels that are out of alignment
one suspension clamp had lost its grip
the braking system worked but was clogged with grime
the road test after repair showed no sway at all
the driver had been running like that for weeks
text: A driver left his trailer with us on a wet evening, reporting an odd sway that showed up as soon as the speed climbed. We worked through it station by station. First station: the coupling ball, whose play ran well past the allowed tolerance, enough on its own to set the whole rig lurching over a crowned road surface. Second station: the tires, worn on a slant along the inner edge, which is the classic mark of wheels out of alignment. Third station: the leaf suspension, where one clamp had lost its torque altogether. Fourth station: the brake circuit, sound in itself but clogged with grime. We fitted a fresh ball, reset the axle, drew the clamps up again and bled the lines. On the road test the sway had gone, and the driver admitted he had been running like that for a whole season.

units: the first check bears on how hard the tires are inflated
a soft tire slips on wet ground
the drive train must be looked over next
the braking surfaces have to stay free of damp
the saddle is set so the leg comes almost straight at the bottom of the stroke
the bags are spread on either side of the rear wheel
an uneven load makes the ride unsteady on a slope
you take along what is needed to mend a puncture
a brake test comes before you join the traffic
text: Before setting out, kindly work through the following steps in the order given here. Begin with the tires and squeeze each one firmly between thumb and forefinger, since soft rubber slips on a wet road surface. Look the chain over next and check its tension along its whole run, then turn to the brake pads, whose faces must stay clean and dry. Set the saddle height so that the leg comes almost straight at the bottom of the pedal stroke. Load the bags on either side of the rear wheel and balance the weight carefully between them. An uneven load will set the machine weaving on the very first descent. Take along a spare inner tube, two tire levers and a hand pump. Finish with a short trial run on level ground, squeezing the brakes gradually as you go, and only then join the traffic.

units: a crossing structure has been taken out of service for repair
vehicles now use a narrow road along the heights
trucks have trouble passing one another there
the time spent commuting has doubled
the buses that carry people together are running late
shops in the lower quarter are losing custom
the local authority has put link boats into service
this arrangement does not settle the matter of freight
the metal frame had been eaten away by corrosion
completion is expected before the cold season ends
text: Closing the bridge for repairs has thrown traffic across the whole town into disorder. Vehicles now climb a narrow ridge road where heavy trucks struggle to pass one another. The effect came at once: journeys between home and workshop take twice as long, and the buses that gather workers arrive behind schedule. Shopkeepers in the lower quarter report a clear drop in custom, since people give up on the detour. The local authority answered by chartering two river shuttles, which link the banks at close intervals. The stopgap takes in a share of the walkers, but it leaves the question of deliveries untouched. An engineer on the site explains that the steel frame had been eaten away by corrosion and that no partial repair would have held. Work should finish before the cold season ends.

units: the access track is made of gravel and looks to be in poor shape
it climbs steeply and forks at the top
the hollows in the ground shake vehicles violently
rain makes the surface slippery
the wheels lose their grip as the bend comes up
a man living nearby decided to act
he brought in crushed stone to fill the holes
he opened a drainage ditch along the bank
the ground now dries out quickly
dust rises when towed vehicles go past
text: Honestly, our gravel track has never been much to look at. It climbs steeply, it turns hard at the fork up top, and the ruts run so deep that the car pitches about like an old rowboat on a swell. In the rain the surface turns to soap and the wheels let go just before the bend, so you grip the wheel with both hands and hope that nothing is coming down at you. The man at the bottom of the hill finally had enough of it. He hauled in a whole load of crushed stone, filled the hollows one by one, then cut a channel along the bank to carry the water off. Since then the slope dries out fast and the mud no longer builds up. It is not perfect. Dust flies up the moment a trailer goes past, but at last we drive up there without fear. The mail carrier still leaves his van below and walks up.

units: the piece sets road widening against the growth of rail
a line of cars takes up a wide strip for few passengers
a train on rails moves as many people in less space
those who defend the car point to its being always available
that advantage counts above all where few people live
towns that widened their main roads see congestion return
this return of saturation happens very quickly
a service running at steady intervals takes in the rise in numbers
the writer urges spending first on the lasting answer
text: Should we widen the expressways once more, or pay for extra train sets? The question deserves a cool head. A line of private cars takes up a great width of ground to shift a handful of people, while a train on rails carries the same crowd within a far narrower strip. Drivers reply that a car goes anywhere, at any hour, with no connection to catch and no waiting about. The point holds, above all outside the crowded districts. Yet towns that have doubled their main roads watch the flow fill the widened lanes to the brim within a single season. A service running at steady intervals, by contrast, takes in the growth without choking. Our stand is plain: widening relieves briefly, frequent service relieves for good. Public money would do better to fund what does not clog up again.
